messages.content: You are a production engineer. Give a concise, structured answer without exposing hidden reasoning.

Design an incident triage checklist for a streaming language-model API whose users report slow first tokens while tokens arrive normally afterward. The system has a client, an API gateway, a model server, and one model on a single machine. Distinguish evidence that points to client networking, gateway queueing, prompt tokenization and prefill, or model decoding. Include the minimum timestamps and counters needed to isolate the stage, explain why end-to-end latency alone is insufficient, and describe one controlled test using short and long prompts at concurrency one and four. Discuss how prefix caching might distort the test and how to prevent that. State how time to first token differs from time per output token and inter-token latency. End with a brief decision tree that an on-call engineer could follow. Do not invent observed measurements and do not recommend scaling until the bottleneck is identified.
You are a production engineer. Give a concise, structured answer without exposing hidden reasoning.

Write a deployment-readiness review for a small LLM service on a memory-constrained machine. Cover request validation, maximum prompt and output sizes, streaming disconnects, cancellation propagation, bounded concurrency, queue limits, overload responses, startup and readiness behavior, model revision pinning, artifact hashes, structured logs, metrics cardinality, traces, secrets, graceful shutdown, reproducibility, and rollback. For every topic, give one concrete acceptance criterion that can be tested. Separate correctness checks from performance checks. Explain why a successful single request is not evidence of production readiness and why dashboards cannot replace raw benchmark records. Keep the plan suitable for one machine; do not add Kubernetes, a message broker, or a new observability stack.
You are a production engineer. Give a concise, structured answer without exposing hidden reasoning.

Compare two deployments of the same language model: native 16-bit weights and 4-bit quantized weights. Define a fair experiment that can attribute differences to quantization rather than prompt choice, generation randomness, cache state, concurrency, background load, or different server code. Specify what metadata must be recorded, how warm-up and measured runs must be separated, how model load time and peak memory should be sampled, and how errors and timeouts affect percentiles and throughput. Explain which quality checks can be scored objectively and when an LLM judge would be only heuristic. Include safeguards against silently comparing different tokenizer revisions or chat templates. Finish with a list of invalid comparison patterns to reject.
